Known bugs get the same fix, every time.

Not a guess anymore — rules you wrote, judged by tests you own. fluidfix repairs known error classes deterministically: no model in the loop, no external tools, no network — the same input produces the same byte-exact fix in CI, on a laptop, or air-gapped. Show it a class once; it fixes every member the same way forever. Anything outside your rules is refused loudly, never guessed — with the failing test that killed each rejected fix on record.

the problem, in numbers engineers already cite

Maintenance is not a side quest. It is most of the job.

None of these numbers are ours — they are the industry's own measurements. fluidfix exists because a measurable slice of this spend is structural: the same small bug shapes, shipped again and again, each one burning an engineer-hour to triage and fix by hand.

42%

of developer time goes to maintenance

13.5 h/week on technical debt plus 3.8 h on bad code, out of a 41.1-hour week — ~$300B/year of lost capacity. Stripe, The Developer Coefficient

~50%

of programming time is finding & fixing bugs

$312B/year of global debugging cost — a quarter of the world's software wage bill. Cambridge Judge Business School

$2.41T

cost of poor software quality — US alone, one year

Including ~$1.52T of accumulated technical debt. CISQ 2022 report

16 shapes

cover a third of single-statement bug fixes

153,652 single-statement fixes mined from 1,000 top open-source projects: ~33% match just 16 syntactic templates — about one such bug per 1,600–2,500 lines of code. Those templates are exactly what fluidfix calls fault classes. ManySStuBs4J, MSR

And our own measured slice, so you can compare like with like: across 10 real codebases (~20,000 commits scanned) we counted 3.6–22 one-line bug fixes shipped per repo per year that made it into history — a lower bound, since regressions caught before merge never appear as commits. High-churn software that fights a moving world (scrapers, adapters, integrations) sits at the top of that range. Every protocol and raw log: docs/SCALE.md.

how it works

A four-instruction kernel decides. Your suite judges.

The decision layer is a machine-authored, exhaustively verified expression — not a model, not a lookup table. Run fluidfix selfcheck and re-derive every law on your machine in about a second.

Five laws, one system, and each one earned its place by fixing a measured failure: fluid-router decides which repair — four integer instructions, all 4,096 cases verified. fluid-router2 drives which candidate next, with termination proved. dev (the engine law) derives what to do next — one controller that generalises across four different jobs, proved by an exhaustive sweep (0 of 256 situations rule differently); vendored verbatim and fingerprint-tested. The ranking law orders which line first, and the SIGHT law orders which file first — the two that decide whether fluidfix ever opens the right file at all. All five re-derive on your machine in about a second. What each one is for →

01

Localise

Traceback frames ∪ failing-test coverage ∪ AST spans find the fault file and line. Mechanical, zero tokens.

02

Route

The kernel maps the observed fault class to its repair from ONE worked example.

act = 15 & ((x>>4) + ((x>>8) − x))
03

Judge

Your own test suite accepts or rejects every candidate. Rejected candidates roll back byte-exact.

04

Refuse

Empty mask → loud refusal, untouched tree, and a machine-readable teach-me signal. Never a plausible guess.

deterministic

Same bug, same fix — provably

The decision is four integer instructions, not a model: no temperature, no drift, no prompt. Run fluidfix selfcheck and re-derive every law on your own machine — all five laws, 4,096 routing cases, identity, composition, termination — in about a second. Reproducible fixes are auditable fixes.

yours

Your rules, your tests, your repo

Fault classes are versioned files in YOUR repo, written from YOUR incidents, judged by YOUR suite — nothing leaves the machine, no vendor in the decision path. On 33 real-library bugs the rules beat a frontier model debugging freely: 26/27 byte-exact vs 22/27 — and the model shipped five suite-green-but-different edits; the rules shipped zero.

honesty

Refusal under contract

Green suite: touches nothing. Unknown class: refuses, exits 2, writes the teach-me report. The failure mode is a statement, not a wrong edit.

what it fixes — honestly

You teach rules, not values.

fluidfix learns a whole bug class from one example when the fix is a rule you apply to the broken line. When a fix needs a value that isn't on the line, it refuses instead of guessing. Both columns below are from a real generalisation test — one example taught, then run on different, unseen bugs of the same class.

generalises from one example ✓

Rule-shaped fixes

Flipped >= / >, swapped + / −, off-by-one literals, and/or, True/False, ==/!=, a .get() missing its default, swapped return operands. One example = the whole class, free forever.

Tested: 11/11 unseen bugs repaired byte-exact.

refused, never guessed ✗

Value-shaped fixes

The right variable name, the right constant, the right guard for this function — information the broken line doesn't carry. One example of name→email can't know the next bug is count→total. fluidfix leaves these for a human.

Tested: 0/5 — every one safely refused, zero wrong edits.

That refusal is the product: an unattended repair tool is only trustworthy if its failure mode is a loud "not this one," never a silent wrong edit. Measured record across every test: many repairs, zero wrong ones.

one example, measured

Teach a class once. Here's exactly how far that goes.

Each class was taught from one worked example, then tested on different, held-out bugs of the same class. These results are enforced as tests in the repo's CI — if they stop being true, the build goes red.

Class shapeHeld-out bugsResult
Rule-shaped — flipped +/−, comparison strictness, off-by-one literals, missing .get default… 11 bugs · 4 classes 11/11 repaired byte-exact
Value-shaped, repo-searchable — the wrong attribute, name, or constant, where the correct value exists somewhere in your repo: fluidfix mines the candidates and your suite judges each one. One registration covered .name→.id and .count→.total — different values, same class. Scale caveat, measured: the candidate set is bounded (32 by default, --max-candidates raises it) because every candidate costs a suite run. In a small module the right name is found in seconds; in a 200,000-line codebase it can rank in the thousands, and then fluidfix refuses rather than guess — see the note below. held-out set repaired byte-exact
Value not in the repo — the right answer was a computation that exists nowhere in the codebase. 1 case every candidate failed → refused, tree byte-identical

The boundary, stated plainly (measured on SQLAlchemy — 18,270 commits, 21 years, 201k lines). What decides whether one example pays off is not how often a bug class recurs, it is how big the candidate set is. Rule-shaped classes have one answer (“add the missing default”), so one example covers the whole family forever. Value-shaped classes have as many answers as your file has names: replaying 38 real historical bugs, the maintainer’s exact fix was generated for 25 of them — but at ranks 42 to 10,563, so the default budget stops first and the guard refuses with the tree untouched. Raising --max-candidates reaches more of them when your suite is cheap. We publish this because it is the honest way to know what to expect from your repo before you pay for anything.

And at large-repo scale — strict, seeded, no cherry-picking

Random mechanical bugs injected at seeded sites across three big codebases; the guard was never told which file. Both held-out repos beat the one the fixes were tuned on. Full protocol, raw logs, and every miss autopsied: docs/SCALE.md.

RepoSizeByte-exactRefused (safe)Wrong repairs
click28,581 LOC · 1,990 tests3/6 + 1 suite-passing20
arrow (held-out)19,928 LOC · 1,902 tests5/610
sortedcontainers (held-out)11,324 LOC · 366 tests6/600
total18 live trials14/18 byte-exact (78%)3 — each with a named cause0 · and 3/3 novel-class bugs refused

Big-repo repairs take seconds to minutes (median ≈ 3 min; the suite is re-run for every candidate). Precise wording we stand by: fluidfix never ships a repair your suite rejects; byte-exactness is bounded by your suite's strength — 14 of 15 accepted repairs here restored the original code exactly.

The contract underneath all three rows: fluidfix has never made a wrong repair — every fix passes your full suite or is rolled back byte-for-byte, and what it can't prove, it refuses. Precision is bounded by your suite's strength, which is also why it rewards teams that test.

v0.9.1: know your repair time before you install

Repair time is not a mystery and it is not our number — it is suite runs × your suite's own runtime. Test count barely matters: 105 tests that run in 0.07s are cheaper to guard than 20 tests that take 5s. One command measures your repo and tells you, before you commit to anything:

fluidfix estimate .
reposuitepredictedactual
toy fixture2 tests @ 0.01s~1.1s1.1s
RPG engine (independent tester)105 tests @ 0.07s1.4–7s1.7s
click 8.5.11,990 tests @ 4.5s12.2–61s36s and 50s

The model was validated, not asserted: both real repairs landed inside the band predicted from their suite alone. The arithmetic is time ≈ runs × (suite time + startup) — nothing else in fluidfix costs measurable wall clock, because the kernels decide in nanoseconds. Your tests are the entire bill. The timing model came from an independent third-party tester who built a 105-test engine specifically to probe the middle of the curve; estimate ships their finding as a command.

v0.6: a third law took every miss back

The guard is now governed by a machine-authored decision law. When a search was budget-truncated, it escalates — bounded by a wall clock. When two different fixes both pass your suite, it refuses and asks for one pinning test — it never guesses. And when nothing was truncated, it stops and says exactly why. Every v0.5 miss above was then replayed byte-for-byte under the law:

v0.5 missv0.5 verdictv0.6 verdict
click/_textwrap.py:18refusedbyte-exact repair · default budget
click/termui.py:744suite-passing, not byte-exactbyte-exact repair · default budget
click/utils.py:70refusedbyte-exact repair · raised budget (--escalate-budget 1800)
arrow/locales.py:5468refusedbyte-exact repair · default budget — the failing test's own name led the search to the line

All four former misses now restore the original bytes — the last one fell when v0.6.1 taught the search what test names already say: TestOdiaLocale::test_ordinal_number points straight at OdiaLocale._ordinal_number, line 5,468 of a 6,500-line file, repaired in 3 suite runs. Raw replay logs, the exact injection scripts, and the full lab notebook — including one contaminated round we caught, discarded, and documented — ship in the repo: docs/data/scale.

students & open source

Free for your repos. Forever.

fluidfix is open source (AGPL) — students, hobby projects, and open source pay nothing, ever. No tests? No problem: fluidfix init . generates a starter suite that guards every module against import-breaking bugs — so any repo is guardable in three commands: pip install --upgrade fluidfix pytest pytest-cov → fluidfix init . → fluidfix guard . --commit. Already have a pytest suite? Even better — three steps: Never written a test? The quickstart teaches you the whole idea in 2 minutes — call your function, check the answer.

step 1

Install & verify

pip install --upgrade fluidfix
fluidfix selfcheck

Selfcheck re-proves the whole engine on your machine in about a second — expect SELFCHECK PASS.

step 2

Guard your repo

cd your-project
fluidfix guard . --commit

Green tests: it touches nothing. A mechanical bug: it finds the file itself, repairs it byte-exact, and commits fluidfix: restore …. An unknown bug: it refuses loudly — that one's yours to fix, and honestly, that's the good practice.

step 3

Guard it on GitHub

Add .github/workflows/fluidfix.yml — repairs don't just pass CI, they land on the branch:

name: fluidfix
on: [push]
jobs:
  guard:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: {python-version: "3.12"}
      - run: pip install -e . pytest pytest-cov   # your project's deps
      - uses: devkancheti4-design/fluidfix@master
        # repairs are PUSHED BACK to the branch (permissions: contents: write)
        # refusals fail the job with every rejected candidate + the test
        # that killed it in the job summary — live proof:
        # github.com/devkancheti4-design/fluidfix-action-demo

what's actually inside

Five machine-authored laws. Not one of them written by a human.

fluidfix is not a model with a prompt. Every decision it makes comes from a small integer law authored by a synthesis engine from measured examples. Each one exists because something measurably failed without it — the incident is named on every card. Re-derive all five on your own machine in about a second with fluidfix selfcheck.

decides

fluid-router — which repair

route(F1,A1,Fq) = (Fq+A1−F1) mod 16, four integer instructions. Verified on all 4,096 cases plus identity and composition.

Why: a fault class must cost one worked example, not a rule per instance. The router infers each class's act from that single example, so teaching is one register() call and renumbering your classes breaks nothing.

drives

fluid-router2 — which candidate next

EMIT, ADVANCE, HALT over a fault-kind mask. All 256 dispatch states checked.

Why: a repair loop that can't prove it stops is a repair loop that hangs in your CI. Termination is proved, not hoped for: every mask drains.

derives & generalises

dev — the engine law — what to do next

act = (4 & ntzb(x−7)) + ntzb(x + (x&128)) — authored in 2.9 seconds from 22 measured events, exact on all 22. Vendored verbatim; a test pins it to the dev repo's published fingerprint (sha256 48bf50bf…, 1,555 chars).

It generalises, structurally. One controller governs four different jobs — write code, answer a question, debug, review a PR — and the job lives in bits it cannot see. Swept exhaustively: 0 of 256 situations rule differently across those four jobs. It generalises because it never looks at which job it is in.

And it derives fixes, not just verdicts. Eight observations map to eight acts: ship, add state, add material, reshape, change granularity, raise budget, harvest the counterexample, author a successor. Two of those rulings became fluidfix features because the law called for them: CHANGE_GRANULARITY is why repairs can edit a multi-line span atomically, and HARVEST_COUNTEREXAMPLE is why every rejected candidate is logged with the test that killed it. The law told the product what to build.

fluidfix measures 5 of the 8 observations today; NOTWIN, HIDDEN and SELF are never set — a documented limitation, not an accident.

orders lines

the ranking law — which line first

Seven evidence lanes over one observation byte, with RETRIED as a veto. 256/256 against spec, veto dominance and monotonicity both hold.

Why: measured 2026-09-02 on click — a taught class that had just repaired two instances of itself spent 1,934s and 474 rejected candidates on a third without ever opening the defect file. Line order was hand-written heuristics; it was the whole gap. With the law and the failure's own literals as evidence, that repair went 1,740s failing → 50s byte-exact.

orders files

the SIGHT law — which file first

Eight lanes in two tiers. R1: pointing evidence outranks circumstantial evidence at any quantity. R2: the ubiquity penalty cannot reach a pointed-at file. Both hold algebraically, not by a comparison someone could write backwards. 0 violations on all 256 inputs; 1.22 ns per candidate file.

Why: measured 2026-09-03 on click — a defect in types.py whose failing tests lived in test_shell_completion.py. Because click has a shell_completion.py, a filename coincidence outranked real evidence and the defect file was ranked 6th, then deprioritised again for being touched by every test. 209 candidates, budget gone, refused. The law makes that inversion unrepresentable.

authors

proven-reason — the engine behind them

Give it examples; it authors the smallest expression reproducing every one, then a decider checks all 4,294,967,296 int32 inputs.

Why: it derives what has not been written — and says so when nothing in its material can reach the answer. That refusal is the reason these laws can be trusted.

The fusion is audited, not asserted. fluidfix selfcheck re-derives all five laws from scratch — no network, no dependencies — and fluidfix's copy of the engine law is byte-identical to the dev repo's, agrees with it on all 1,024 situations, and rules exactly on all 22 measured events. A test parses every "engine law: X → Y" claim in the shipped source and re-derives it from the law itself, so a comment can never drift from the ruling it names. Each law is attached at exactly one granularity — the ranking law orders lines, the SIGHT law orders files — and tests pin that too.

pricing

Priced by what your repo actually breaks.

Not by seats, not by lines of code. We scanned 10 real codebases (~20,000 commits) and counted the mechanical one-line fixes each one really shipped per year — the work fluidfix takes over. Repo type predicts that rate, so type sets the rate card below, and a free scan of your repo either confirms your tier or moves you down. The scan can only lower your price, never raise it.

Repo typeMeasured one-line fixes / yearPer repo / month
Library / stable
datetime, locale, crypto utilities		 3.6–4.0 (arrow, babel, paramiko) $9
Service / framework
web apps, APIs, CLIs, internal services		 4.4–6.3 (flask, httpx, tqdm, requests, click) $19
Adapter / integration
scrapers, connectors, parsers, data generators — anything fighting a moving world		 8.7–22.1 (faker, yt-dlp) $49
Enterprise fleet
every repo typed and scanned, then rolled up		 your mix, measured from $499/mo

Every tier is roughly a quarter of the low end of what that repo type costs in engineer time at $100/hr — so you keep about 4× what you pay before counting anything history can't see (regressions caught before merge never become commits).
